title: Merge Overlapping Ranges
statement:
You get a list of ranges, ranges[i] = [start, end], each covering every number from start to end inclusive. The list is in no particular order.

Merge every group of ranges that overlap or touch (share an end point, like [2, 5] and [5, 7]) into one range. Return the merged ranges sorted by start.

examples.why: [1, 4] and [3, 5] overlap, and so do [8, 10] and [9, 12]. Neighbours in the input are not the ones that overlap, so sort first.
[1, 10] swallows both others. Taking the end of the last range merged in (6) instead of the largest end gives the wrong [1, 6].
[7, 7] touches [5, 7] and merges. [1, 2] and [5, 7] have a gap, so they stay apart.

hints: Two ranges can overlap even when they are far apart in the input. What ordering would put ranges that might merge next to each other?
After sorting by start, a range can only merge with the block you are currently building, never with something earlier.
Sort by start. Keep the last merged block. If the next range starts at or before that block's end, extend the end to the larger of the two ends; otherwise start a new block.

explain.intuition:
Overlap is hard to see in an unsorted list. Once the ranges are sorted by start, it becomes a single sweep from left to right. Keep the block you are building. The next range either starts at or before that block's end, in which case it joins (it starts no earlier than the block, so it can only push the end further out), or it starts after the end, in which case no later range can reach back to the block either, because later ranges start even further right. So the block is finished and a new one begins.

When a range joins, the new end is the maximum of the two ends, because a later range can sit entirely inside an earlier one. It is the same idea as collapsing overlapping highlight ranges in a text editor before rendering them.
steps: Start the output with the first range.
For each next range [s, e]: if s ≤ last[1], set last[1] = max(last[1], e).
Otherwise push [s, e] as a new block.
Return the output, which is already sorted by start.
pitfalls: Merging only ranges that are neighbours in the input, without sorting. Example 1 breaks that.
Setting the end to the new range's end instead of the max. Example 2 shows a nested range shrinking the block.
Using s < last[1], which keeps touching ranges apart.

complexity.space: O(n) for the sorted copy and the output

solutions.title: Absorb into a set of disjoint blocks
solutions.idea: Keep a list of blocks that never overlap. For each range, pull out every block it overlaps or touches, widen the range to cover them, and put it back. Sort at the end.

solutions.title: Sort by start, then sweep
solutions.idea: After sorting, each range either extends the current block or starts a new one.

followups: Ranges arrive one at a time and you must keep the merged list up to date after each. What structure keeps each insert fast?
Return the total length covered by the ranges. Do you need to build the merged list at all?
